newsitem.title: USA: Copper hits 2-1/2 month high on strike-related outages.
newsitem.headline: Copper hits 2-1/2 month high on strike-related outages.

text.p: Copper prices jumped to their highest level in 2-1/2 months Friday, boosted by a mine workers' strike in Chile and a strike-related smelter outage in Namibia.
Crude oil prices edged higher but cotton, gold and wheat prices fell, and the Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 commodities lost 0.20 points to 249.46.
Dealers said copper's rise was fuelled by aggressive buying by traders squaring their books ahead of the long holiday weekend and growing concern about the supply disruptions.
Workers at the Salvador copper mine in Chile went on strike Friday, demanding wage increases and other benefits. Chile is the world's largest copper producer.
In Namibia, Gold Fields Namibia Ltd. said that the copper smelter at its subsidiary Tsumeb Corp. could be closed for six weeks or longer through damage caused by striking workers.
"The market is going to remain very tight through the middle of September at the very least," said Dean Witter's Mike Frawley, adding there had also been strong demand in the Far East.

Copper for December delivery rose 4.55 cents to 95.25 cents a pound at New York's Commodity Exchange after hitting 95.78 cents during the session. That was the highest since the December contract touched 98.80 cents on June 13.
Cotton closed lower as speculators opted to sell ahead of the long weekend as the threat that hurricanes could hit key growing areas receded.

"The weather forecasters were saying that hurricanes were not going to affect the cotton growing areas so the speculators jumped out before the long weekend and took profits from the last six days," one trader said.

Hurricane Edouard lost strength and turned north on Friday, lessening its threat to the Atlantic Coast. Hurricane Fran and tropical storm Gustav were still far from land, the National Hurricane Centre said.
December cotton fell 0.72 cent to 76.34 cents a pound at the New York Cotton Exchange.
Gold prices fell despite inflation jitters on Wall Street that sent bond and stock prices lower and long-term interest rates further above the 7 percent level.
"It's a bit discouraging that precious metals got no support from the nervousness in debt and equity markets, but Japanese disinvestment looks to be continuing," Refco's analyst James Steel said.
The December contract fell $1.10 to $391.30 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange, after touching $390, its lowest in nearly a month.
Wheat prices also fell amid forecasts that world production will rise this year.
The International Grain Council Friday pegged 1996 world wheat output at 563 million metric tons, up from the previous forecast for 560 million tons.
"The IGC estimate wasn't a shock but there's nothing bullish in it," one trader said.
Slow exports and good harvest weather for spring wheat also depressed prices. September wheat lost 2-3/4 cents to $4.48-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Oil markets were mixed in quiet trading with profit-taking on products after their recent strong advance.

September heating oil fell 0.85 cent to 62.82 cents a gallon and September unleaded gasoline slipped 0.90 cents to 62.82 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. October crude oil, however, rose 10 cents to $22.25 a barrel.
